title: Gantert's Question
statement_text: Let $G$ be a connected graph and let $r,v\in V(G)$. If $w\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{V(G)}$ is edge-reachable from $\mathds{1}_{\{r\}}$, must we have $w(v)\leq\frac{1}{d_{G}(r,v)+1}$?
context_text: The SAD-procedure (Sharing A Drink), introduced by Häggström, repeatedly equalises weights along edges of a graph. Nina Gantert asked whether the weight at any vertex $v$ reachable from a single unit at $r$ is bounded above by $1/(d_G(r,v)+1)$. The paper's first main result, Theorem 1.1, resolves this question affirmatively and shows the bound is tight.
paper_contribution: Proves the bound $w(v)\leq\frac{1}{d_{G}(r,v)+1}$ for all graphs $G$ and all weight distributions edge-reachable from a single unit at $r$, and extends it to arbitrary sharing moves via Corollary 1.2; the bound is shown to be best possible.
notes: Gantert's question is a personal communication (2024), not a published paper.

title: Question 6.1
statement_text: For every finite graph $G$, every ${w\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{V(G)}}$, and every ${v\in V(G)}$, is there always a ${(w,v)}$-optimal sequence whose length is at most $2^{{\left\lvert{V(G)}\right\rvert}}$?
context_text: A weight distribution on $G$ is a function $w\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{V(G)}$ (the amount of tea at each vertex). A sharing move on a finite nonempty set $T\subseteq V(G)$ inducing a connected subgraph replaces $w(x)$ by the average $w(T)/|T|$ for every $x\in T$ and leaves other vertices unchanged. With $\mathcal{R}(w)$ the set of distributions reachable from $w$ by finite sequences of sharing moves, $w^*(v)=\sup\{w'(v):w'\in\mathcal{R}(w)\}$, and a finite sequence $(T_1,\dots,T_m)$ of sharing moves is $(w,v)$-optimal if applying it to $w$ yields a distribution $w'$ with $w'(v)=w^*(v)$. The authors prove that starting from one unit of tea at a vertex $r$, a vertex at distance $d$ never gets more than $1/(d+1)$ (attained by one sharing move along a shortest path), and that for every finite graph a $(w,v)$-optimal sequence always exists (whereas on infinite graphs it may not); but it is unclear whether the length of a shortest optimal sequence is bounded by a computable function of $|V(G)|$, even for $w\in\{0,1\}^{V(G)}$, and they do not know how to prove existence without the Axiom of Choice. One approach to a positive answer would be to show that some optimal sequence never repeats a sharing move; however, there is a finite tree with a distribution $w$ and vertex $v$ for which every optimal sequence contains a move that is a subset of a later move.
